title: Aurora teen, shot and killed by 4 York Region officers, 'lured' cops to his home as part of plan to kill them: SIU
subtitle: The SIU, which reviews police conduct in Ontario, announced on Feb. 25 four York Region officers who fired an estimated 50 shots at the 17-year-old boy will not face any charges.
article: An Aurora teenager, who was killed in a barrage of police gunfire last fall, likely lured the officers to his home as part of a plan to kill cops, said the Special Investigations Unit (SIU).
The SIU, which reviews police conduct in Ontario, announced on Feb. 25 four York Region officers who fired an estimated 50 shots at the 17-year-old boy will not face any charges.
Ontario's police watchdog did not identify the youth, however the Toronto Star has identified him as Mikail Rashid.

The officers responded to a residential address on Downey Circle around 7:30 p.m., on Oct. 30, after the teen called 911. According to the SIU, the 17-year-old asked police to come to his home because he heard shouting and banging on his door and noises in his garage.
The teen "spoke very quickly and repeatedly asked how far away the police were," said the SIU report.
The call, wrote SIU director Joseph Martino, appeared to be a way for the teen to set a trap for police.

"For whatever reason, it seems the (teenager) had set in motion a plan to lure police to his home where it appeared he intended to shoot and kill officers responding to a fake report of a break and enter in progress," said Martino in the report.

The first officer to respond to the break-in call was met with heavy gunfire when the teenager fired "upwards of 20 rounds" from a rifle inside the home, the SIU report said. The cop ran for cover and was not hit or injured.
Shortly after that first wave of gunfire, the teen emerged from his home wearing a tactical vest and holding a shotgun, said the SIU.
When another officer at the scene ordered the teen to drop his weapon, the 17-year-old told the officer to shut up and threatened to kill him, the report said.
At that point, the SIU said the teen fired several rounds from the shotgun and the second officer was hit in the face by a pellet.

The teen then moved along the street with the shotgun and was again ordered by other officers to drop his weapon. In response, he swore at the cops and fired another shot in their direction, said the SIU.
That prompted a third officer to return fire with her pistol, which struck the teen and knocked him down, the SIU report said.

The teenager then returned to his feet and, now armed with a machete, began to advance on the officers. That led to the four officers, whose actions were scrutinized by the SIU, to fire "multiple rounds" at the teenager, the police watchdog's report said.

The teen was once again hit and knocked down by the gunfire. When he rolled to his right, in the direction of the dropped machete, the four officers fired "a second volley of shots" at the teen, said the SIU.
The 17-year-old "fell back and did not move again," the SIU report said. He was then handcuffed and later declared dead at the scene.
According to a preliminary autopsy report, the teen's death was "attributable to multiple gunshot wounds."
The SIU report stated, "10 projectiles and a fragment were removed from the (teen) during post-mortem examination."
Following the shooting, the SIU's investigators recovered 45 shell cases fired by officers' C8 rifles and four 9-mm shell cases from a police pistol.

A pump-action shotgun and live shells, as well as seven discharged shotgun shells, were also located. Inside the teen's home, the SIU said a .22-calibre rifle as well as "numerous" .22-shell casings were found on the floor under a damaged window.
In his report summary, Martino noted the only officer of the four under scrutiny who agreed to be interviewed by the SIU told investigators he believed the machete was a long gun.

"It was dark, the (teen) had just been seen holding and firing a long gun at the officers and he carried and was reaching for a long slender object that I am satisfied might credibly have been misconstrued for a firearm," wrote Martino.

"I am unable to reasonably conclude that any of the (officers) fired their weapons without believing it was necessary to do so to protect themselves from a reasonably apprehended attack," the director added. "The officers' lives were in immediate peril and it was imperative that the (teenager) be incapacitated as quickly as possible."
Martino also described the number of shots fired by the officers as "high," but stressed the amount "did not exceed" what was reasonable in the circumstances.
"The gunfire occurred in rapid succession over three distinct phases during which the officers were either being shot at or reasonably believed they were about to be fired on," wrote Martino.
